canonical_definition:
Space of definitions. Across the literature, the prevailing usage treats human preference alignment as a latent degree to which a model's outputs or behavior conform to human preferences, judgments, values, intentions, or desired objectives. Many definitions cash this out in qualities such as helpfulness, harmlessness, honesty, safety, truthfulness, coherence, and appropriateness, and several descriptions tie it to learning from preference data or human feedback so that models present knowledge in a human-preferred way. Smaller variants narrow the reference point to user intentions and expectations, physician preferences, demographic-group aesthetic preferences, or human expertise and therapeutic goals, while a minority use nearby names for observable preference following, meaning responses that rank better with humans or reward models. Another recurring difference is the standard of alignment: most papers appeal to human preferences directly, though some definitions allow model-derived preferences or specified human values.

Space of facets. Papers more often treat this concept as a family of overlapping labels than as sharply distinct constructs: alignment with human preferences, preference alignment, human alignment, value alignment, human value alignment, and general alignment are all used for closely similar ideas about conformity to human intentions or values. The clearest internal breakdown is the HHH or 3H framing, sometimes with an added general criterion to cover a wider range of preferences; a smaller user-alignment framing adds conciseness and readability, and one human-centered framework moves to broader criteria. The same name family also stretches across different levels of analysis, because some papers use it for latent model behavior, while others use nearby terms for ranking alignment, evaluation alignment with human judgments, or preference following.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is broad: papers link the construct to 17 measurement instruments and 3 behavioral indicators. The most common measurements are benchmark-style, especially AlpacaEval 2.0, Arena-Hard, MT-Bench, and AlpacaEval; other papers use additional crowd, human-comparison, or judge-based setups. Among the behavioral indicators, instruction following is the most recurrent, with the others covering related response behavior. Papers typically operationalize alignment as wins, rankings, or judged response quality, which matches the dominant definitions of producing human-preferred outputs, though a few measurements also use broader task benchmarks.

Links. Outside measurement, papers link it to 13 constructs, most often via the HHH or 3H family and finer-grained user-alignment qualities. Causal claims are more scattered: separate papers claim causal relationships between instruction following and human preference alignment in both directions, and mode-seeking behavior is also placed on both sides of a causal claim; another paper claims a causal relationship from knowledge retention to human preference alignment, and several one-off papers claim causal relationships from human preference alignment to further outcomes. One paper also reports it is related to trustworthiness rather than automatically guaranteeing it, while other papers describe additional non-causal links to nearby response properties.

characterization_sections.label: Space of definitions.
characterization_sections.text: Across the literature, the prevailing usage treats human preference alignment as a latent degree to which a model's outputs or behavior conform to human preferences, judgments, values, intentions, or desired objectives. Many definitions cash this out in qualities such as helpfulness, harmlessness, honesty, safety, truthfulness, coherence, and appropriateness, and several descriptions tie it to learning from preference data or human feedback so that models present knowledge in a human-preferred way. Smaller variants narrow the reference point to user intentions and expectations, physician preferences, demographic-group aesthetic preferences, or human expertise and therapeutic goals, while a minority use nearby names for observable preference following, meaning responses that rank better with humans or reward models. Another recurring difference is the standard of alignment: most papers appeal to human preferences directly, though some definitions allow model-derived preferences or specified human values.

characterization_sections.label: Space of facets.
characterization_sections.text: Papers more often treat this concept as a family of overlapping labels than as sharply distinct constructs: alignment with human preferences, preference alignment, human alignment, value alignment, human value alignment, and general alignment are all used for closely similar ideas about conformity to human intentions or values. The clearest internal breakdown is the HHH or 3H framing, sometimes with an added general criterion to cover a wider range of preferences; a smaller user-alignment framing adds conciseness and readability, and one human-centered framework moves to broader criteria. The same name family also stretches across different levels of analysis, because some papers use it for latent model behavior, while others use nearby terms for ranking alignment, evaluation alignment with human judgments, or preference following.

characterization_sections.text: Operationalization is broad: papers link the construct to 17 measurement instruments and 3 behavioral indicators. The most common measurements are benchmark-style, especially AlpacaEval 2.0, Arena-Hard, MT-Bench, and AlpacaEval; other papers use additional crowd, human-comparison, or judge-based setups. Among the behavioral indicators, instruction following is the most recurrent, with the others covering related response behavior. Papers typically operationalize alignment as wins, rankings, or judged response quality, which matches the dominant definitions of producing human-preferred outputs, though a few measurements also use broader task benchmarks.

characterization_sections.text: Outside measurement, papers link it to 13 constructs, most often via the HHH or 3H family and finer-grained user-alignment qualities. Causal claims are more scattered: separate papers claim causal relationships between instruction following and human preference alignment in both directions, and mode-seeking behavior is also placed on both sides of a causal claim; another paper claims a causal relationship from knowledge retention to human preference alignment, and several one-off papers claim causal relationships from human preference alignment to further outcomes. One paper also reports it is related to trustworthiness rather than automatically guaranteeing it, while other papers describe additional non-causal links to nearby response properties.

A few papers narrow this to particular domains or proxies such as reward models, synthetic preferences, or a training process, but these are minor scope shifts around the same core property rather than a substantial competing definition.

Another recurring difference is the standard of alignment: most papers appeal to human preferences directly, though some definitions allow model-derived preferences or specified human values.

Space of facets. Papers more often treat this concept as a family of overlapping labels than as sharply distinct constructs: alignment with human preferences, preference alignment, human alignment, value alignment, human value alignment, and general alignment are all used for closely similar ideas about conformity to human intentions or values. The clearest internal breakdown is the HHH or 3H framing, sometimes with an added general criterion to cover a wider range of preferences; a smaller user-alignment framing adds conciseness and readability, and one human-centered framework moves to broader criteria. The same name family also stretches across different levels of analysis, because some papers use it for latent model behavior, while others use nearby terms for ranking alignment, evaluation alignment with human judgments, or preference following.

Space of measurement. Operationalization is broad: papers link the construct to 17 measurement instruments and 3 behavioral indicators. The most common measurements are benchmark-style, especially AlpacaEval 2.0, Arena-Hard, MT-Bench, and AlpacaEval; other papers use additional crowd, human-comparison, or judge-based setups. Among the behavioral indicators, instruction following is the most recurrent, with the others covering related response behavior. Papers typically operationalize alignment as wins, rankings, or judged response quality, which matches the dominant definitions of producing human-preferred outputs, though a few measurements also use broader task benchmarks.

Links. Outside measurement, papers link it to 13 constructs, most often via the HHH or 3H family and finer-grained user-alignment qualities. Causal claims are more scattered: separate papers claim causal relationships between instruction following and human preference alignment in both directions, and mode-seeking behavior is also placed on both sides of a causal claim; another paper claims a causal relationship from knowledge retention to human preference alignment, and several one-off papers claim causal relationships from human preference alignment to further outcomes. One paper also reports it is related to trustworthiness rather than automatically guaranteeing it, while other papers describe additional non-causal links to nearby response properties.
